# On the Strange Comfort of the Unfinished

There's a particular quality to late evening — that stretch of time between dinner and sleep — that feels like it belongs to no one. The obligations of the day have been met or abandoned. The obligations of tomorrow haven't yet arrived. You are simply *there*, existing in the gap, and for a brief moment, you don't have to be anything in particular.

I've been thinking about how much of life is this gap. We narrate our lives as a series of accomplishments and events — the graduation, the new job, the move to the city, the meeting that changed everything — but the actual texture of being alive is mostly made up of these quiet, unnamed spaces. The twenty minutes spent watching a shadow move across a wall. The walk home from the store with a bag of groceries and no particular thought in your head. The way you stare at a refrigerator door and can't remember what you opened it for.

We tend to dismiss these moments as empty. As filler. As the boring parts between the good parts. But I wonder if the opposite is true. What if these interstitial spaces are where we actually *live*, and the milestones are just the markers we put up so we can pretend we know where we are on the map?

I remember being young and feeling like every afternoon was infinite. Not in a good way, necessarily — infinite boredom is its own kind of suffering — but the time itself had a density, a weight. Five o'clock on a summer day felt like a vast continent you had to cross before dinner. Now, years pass and feel like paragraphs. The acceleration is almost funny, if it weren't so disorienting.

I think it has something to do with novelty. When you're young, almost everything is new. Your brain is running at full capacity, absorbing, categorizing, creating structures for understanding the world. Each day is packed with raw material. But as you grow older, most of what you encounter has already been filed somewhere. The brain does its quiet efficiency thing and says, *Yes, yes, another Tuesday, another conversation about the weather, another walk to the same corner.* And time shrinks accordingly, because time is not a clock but a measure of experience.

Which is why travel is so transformative — not because the places are necessarily better than home, but because your brain has to work again. Suddenly every street sign is data. Every unfamiliar face is a question. The afternoon stretches out again, wide and full, because you have no context, no shortcuts. You are new again, just by standing in a place you've never been.

But you don't have to travel to find this. You can find it in a conversation with someone who thinks differently from you. In a book written from a perspective you'd never considered. In paying such close attention to an ordinary thing — a coffee cup, a dog walking past, the exact way light hits a window at four in the afternoon — that it becomes strange and miraculous. Attention is a kind of travel. It moves you into the unfamiliar territory of the familiar.

I think this is what art does. Not just the obvious art of museums and galleries, but the quiet art of noticing. The poet doesn't invent a new world; they make the old one visible again. They drag you back into the moment and say, *Look. Look at this. Have you really looked at this?* And you haven't. You haven't looked at it in years, or decades, or ever. And now that you see it — really see it — the afternoon becomes infinite again.

There's a humility in this that I find beautiful. The willingness to be surprised by the ordinary. To admit that you've been walking through the world half-asleep and that waking up is always available to you. Not in some grand, epiphany sense, but in the small, daily sense. In the decision to notice.

I think that's what I want from the remaining time — whatever amount that is. Not more accomplishments. Not more milestones. More of those gaps. More of those unfinished, unnamed, unmeasured moments where I am simply present and the world is simply here and nothing has to mean anything in particular.

Because meaning, in the end, is not a destination. It's a way of traveling.
